scenarios.title: Scenario 1 — Customer Support Resolution Agent
scenarios.brief: A meal-kit company runs a customer support agent on the Claude Agent SDK. Its MCP tools are get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human and pause_subscription. The agent may refund up to $150 per box; larger refunds go to a human.

questions.question: get_customer returns the full card number on file, and the team that owns that server will not change it. Twice, the agent read a card number to a customer. Security says this must never happen. What is the best fix?

options.t: Add a system-prompt rule to mention cards by their last four digits only, with two examples.
options.why: Wrong: only usually works. A prompt rule lowers the chance, but prompts have a non-zero failure rate, and this is a must-never.

options.t: Register a PostToolUse hook that masks the card number in each get_customer result.
options.why: Correct. The hook changes the result before Claude reads it, so the agent can't repeat a number it never saw. The server stays as it is.

options.t: Add a PreToolUse hook that blocks get_customer calls during customer chats.
options.why: Wrong: wrong action. The agent needs get_customer to do its job. Blocking the call breaks support instead of hiding one field.

options.t: Add a PostToolUse hook that logs any card number in a tool result for security to review.
options.why: Wrong: records the leak, doesn't stop it. By the time the log is written, Claude already has the number.

questions.decider: Security says this must never happen.
questions.explanation: When a tool returns data the model must never use, change the result with a PostToolUse hook before the model sees it. Prompt rules only make misuse less likely.

eli5.question: The agent sometimes reads a customer's card number out loud. The clue: security says this must never happen.
eli5.answer: If a receptionist must never read out card numbers, don't hand them the number: black it out on the paper first. A PostToolUse hook is that black marker. It edits each tool result before Claude reads it, and Claude can't repeat what it never saw. Rule: if the model must never use some data, remove it before the model sees it.
options: A written rule usually works, but “usually” isn't enough for a must-never.
Correct. Black out the number before Claude ever sees it.
Blocking the whole lookup means the agent can't help anyone.
A log notices the number but still hands it to Claude.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think a firm instruction stops the model saying something. It lowers the chance, but prompt compliance is probabilistic. For data that must never reach a customer, the reliable place to act is the tool result itself: change it before the model reads it.
deep.diagram:
get_customer → [PostToolUse: mask card] → Claude
server unchanged        model never sees the number

questions.obj: 1.5 Hooks that block outgoing tool calls
questions.question: Refunds above $150 must go to a human. The system prompt says so, yet a monthly review found a few larger refunds that the agent made itself. Finance wants this to stop completely. What should the team do?

options.t: Add a PreToolUse hook that blocks process_refund over $150 and hands the case to a human.
options.why: Correct. The hook checks every refund call before it runs. Code enforces the limit every time, which a prompt can't promise.

options.t: Move the limit to the top of the system prompt and add three examples of refusing larger refunds.
options.why: Wrong: only usually works. Clearer prompting cuts the misses but can't remove them, and finance wants zero.

options.t: Add a PostToolUse hook that flags any refund above the limit in process_refund results for finance.
options.why: Wrong: too late. A PostToolUse hook sees the result after the money has gone.

options.t: Have a second Claude instance review each refund decision before the agent replies to the customer.
options.why: Wrong: still a model's judgement. A reviewer catches some cases but is probabilistic too, and it adds a model call to every refund.

questions.decider: Finance wants this to stop completely.
questions.explanation: Business rules that must hold every time are enforced in code. A PreToolUse hook can inspect each outgoing tool call and block the ones that break the rule.

eli5.question: The agent was told “no refunds over $150”, and still made a few. The clue: finance wants zero.
eli5.answer: Telling a cashier “never give more than $150 back” works most days. A till that won't open above $150 without a manager's key works every day. A PreToolUse hook is that till: it checks the refund before it happens. Rule: must hold every time → check it in code, before the action runs.
options: Correct. The till won't open above the limit.
A bigger sign by the till still relies on the cashier remembering.
Checking the receipt afterwards doesn't bring the money back.
A second cashier watching helps, but can also miss things, and costs more.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think clearer instructions will finish the job. They reduce the misses, but a prompt is followed most of the time, not every time. When the requirement is “never”, put a check in code on the tool call itself, before the action runs.
deep.diagram:
Claude → process_refund($180)
          → [PreToolUse: over $150? deny + escalate]
          → tool never runs
